topics.title: What a non-chord tone is
topics.summary: A non-chord tone (NCT) is a note that does not belong to the current chord. It creates tension and is defined by how it is approached (preparation) and left (resolution).
rules: Consecutive NCTs are not allowed, except when together they form a new chord (moving in 3rds or 6ths).
guidelines: Label the NCT where it sounds (on the note itself).
Several NCTs can sound at once, e.g. a double suspension over V → I6.

topics.title: The dominant seventh: definition and terms
topics.summary: V7 = dom7 = Mm7: a major triad plus a minor 7th above the root. In minor keys the leading tone must be raised.

terms.def: the chord member a 7th above the root (in V7 = 4̂)

rules: In minor, raise the leading tone in V7.

topics.title: Resolving V7: complete and incomplete chords
topics.summary: Moving from V7 to I with all voices resolving normally makes one chord incomplete. Either a complete V7 goes to an incomplete I (5th omitted, root tripled) or an incomplete V7 (5th omitted, root doubled) goes to a complete I.
rules: The leading tone must step up to 1̂ when it is in the soprano or bass.
At most one of the two chords (V7 or I) may be incomplete.
guidelines: In an inner voice the leading tone may leap down to 5̂ so that I is complete (A&S: common in Bach).
In three parts: incomplete V7 (no 5th, root doubled) → chordal 7th resolves.

topics.title: Approaching the chordal 7th
topics.summary: The 7th of V7 (4̂) is a dissonance, so its approach matters as much as its resolution.
rules: Approach the chordal 7th by common tone (prepared like a suspension), by step (passing or neighbour motion) — never by a descending leap.

topics.summary: V and V7 go to I (i) for an authentic cadence or to vi (VI) for a deceptive cadence. Harmonic rhythm tells you whether V–V7 is one chord (V8–7) or two.

topics.title: Summary of V7 and its inversions
topics.summary: Inversions of V7 are almost always complete. Each bass note gives the chord a different job. In the notes' colour code the chordal 7th (4̂) is green and the leading tone (7̂) red.
rules: Chordal 7th 4̂ → 3̂; 3rd (7̂) → 1̂ when in an outer voice; 5th (2̂) moves freely (usually to 1̂ or 3̂); root (5̂) holds or moves to 1̂.
V6/5: the bass is the leading tone and must resolve up to 1̂.
guidelines: Arpeggiating between inversions of V7 (changing inversion without resolving) is allowed.
Inverted dominants sound less cadential than root-position V7.

topics.title: Avoiding a cadential effect mid-phrase
topics.summary: Root-position V(7) → I with 1̂ in the soprano sounds like a cadence. In the middle of a phrase use weaker positions.
guidelines: Use vii°6 or V6 (or V6/5) instead of root-position V(7).
Use I6 (i6) instead of root-position I.

topics.title: Major keys: viiø7 and its inversions
topics.summary: In major the leading-tone seventh is half-diminished (viiø7). It resolves like a dominant: 7̂ up, the 7th (6̂) down, the tritone resolved.
rules: If the soprano has the chordal 7th (6̂) over root-position viiø7, double the 3rd of I to avoid parallel 5ths.
guidelines: viiø4/2 is rare because it lacks the 3rd and P5 above the bass and sounds very dissonant (Dvořák and Tchaikovsky are exceptions).
A frequent use is the neighbour figure 5̂–6̂–5̂ in the soprano over I – viiø7 – I.

topics.title: Minor keys: vii°7 and its inversions
topics.summary: In minor the leading-tone seventh is fully diminished (vii°7, using raised 7̂). Its first three positions correspond to the inversions of V7.
rules: The chordal 7th (♭6̂) resolves down to 5̂; the leading tone resolves up; both tritones resolve (d5 → M3, A4 → m6).
guidelines: Voice-leading options: double the 3rd of i; or let the tritone between the chord's 3rd and 7th resolve irregularly — this produces unequal 5ths (d5 → P5), so check it.
vii°4/2 is the least used position.
